title: Docker & Podman
subtitle: Build an image and run your application in a container.
description: Learn images, containers, and registries, then create a non-root multi-stage Dockerfile. Connect services with Compose, persist data in volumes, and troubleshoot Podman rootless.

lessons.title: Image, container & registry
lessons.summary: An image packages a filesystem and configuration. A container is an isolated process started from that image.
objectives: Identify an image by tag or digest.
Describe the build, push, pull, and run workflow.
keyPoints: One image can start multiple containers.
A container has its own writable layer and shares the host kernel.
Tags can move; a digest identifies fixed image content.
practice: Build an image, push it to a registry, and run it on another host.
The running container uses the tested image digest.

options: One image can run as multiple containers at the same time.
Changing a file inside a container does not change the original image.
A container is a virtual machine with its own kernel.
Writing to a container changes its source image.
exercises.explanation: An image is a reusable read-only base. Each container adds its own writable layer and uses kernel isolation.

exercises.prompt: Which reference best ensures production runs the exact image content that was tested?
options: registry.example.com/order@sha256:3f1c…
registry.example.com/order:latest
registry.example.com/order:0.1
order
exercises.explanation: A digest identifies image content. A tag can be reassigned to different content.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps from source code to a container running on another server.
items: Build an image from the Dockerfile.
Push the image to a registry.
Pull the image on the server.
Run a container from that image.
exercises.explanation: The registry distributes the same image from the build system to runtime hosts.

lessons.title: Dockerfile & non-root processes
lessons.summary: Multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the runtime image. A non-root user limits process privileges.
objectives: Run as a numeric non-root UID.
Use exec-form ENTRYPOINT and explicit port publishing.
keyPoints: Copy only runtime artifacts from the build stage.
An exec-form entrypoint allows the JVM to receive stop signals.
EXPOSE documents a port but does not publish it to the host.
practice: Build a Java 21 runtime image with USER 10001 and an exec-form entrypoint.
The application runs without root and shuts down when it receives SIGTERM.

exercises.prompt: Complete the runtime stage: use eclipse-temurin:21-jre, copy the JAR from build, run as user 10001, and use exec-form ENTRYPOINT.
exercises.explanation: The runtime stage omits Maven and source code. Exec form makes the JVM receive SIGTERM directly.

exercises.prompt: A Dockerfile has EXPOSE 8080. The container starts without -p. Can curl localhost:8080 on the host reach it?
options: No. EXPOSE is documentation; publish the port with -p 8080:8080.
Yes. EXPOSE automatically publishes it.
Yes, but only on Linux.
No, because containers forbid port 8080.
exercises.explanation: Port publication is a runtime setting. Binding to 127.0.0.1 restricts the published port to the local host.

lessons.title: Network, volume & Compose
lessons.summary: Use service names on a shared network and store persistent data outside the container’s writable layer.
objectives: Connect containers through DNS service names.
Persist database data in a volume.
Wait for a database healthcheck during startup.
keyPoints: localhost normally refers to the current container.
depends_on with service_healthy waits for readiness at startup, not every later outage.
practice: Connect Order and PostgreSQL through Compose with a volume and pg_isready healthcheck.
Order uses hostname db and starts after the database is healthy.

exercises.prompt: Configure Compose so order starts after db is healthy. Add a pg_isready healthcheck to db.
checks: Add a db healthcheck using pg_isready
Do not use the simple - db list form
exercises.explanation: The condition waits for the database healthcheck. The application still needs to handle database failures after startup.

exercises.prompt: The app uses jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders, but PostgreSQL is in another container named db. What happens?
options: The connection fails because localhost refers to the app container.
It works because all containers share localhost.
It only works in Podman.
Docker automatically replaces localhost with db.
exercises.explanation: Use db as the hostname on their shared network. Containers only share localhost in configurations such as the same pod.

lessons.title: Podman rootless & troubleshooting
lessons.summary: Run containers without a root daemon and investigate process state, logs, port mappings, and permissions.
objectives: Start Podman’s Linux VM on macOS or Windows.
keyPoints: Podman uses user namespaces in rootless mode.
macOS and Windows need a Linux VM for Linux containers.
Published traffic cannot reach an app listening only on the container’s loopback address.
practice: Run the image with Podman and diagnose a broken port or listen address.
The host reaches the health endpoint through an explicitly published local port.

exercises.prompt: A running order-lab container is unreachable at localhost:8080. Order these diagnostic checks.
items: Check process state with podman ps.
Test inside the container with podman exec order-lab curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health.
exercises.explanation: Check whether the process is running, then distinguish application errors, publication errors, and network access.

exercises.prompt: Which command starts Podman’s Linux VM on macOS?
exercises.hint: Use the machine subcommand followed by start.
exercises.explanation: Initialize the VM once with podman machine init, then start it with podman machine start.

exercises.prompt: The app started on port 8080 and -p is correct, but server.address=127.0.0.1. Why can the host not connect?
options: The app listens only on container loopback; it should listen on 0.0.0.0.
Podman does not support port 8080.
It needs privileged mode.
The image must be pushed to a registry first.
exercises.explanation: Published traffic enters through the container network interface, not its loopback interface.
